item.title: Cancer cases continue to rise as Fiji Cancer Society registers about 217 since January
item.description: Since January this year, 217 people have turned to the Fiji Cancer Society after being diagnosed with cancer, a number that continues to rise year after year. Fiji Cancer Society Board member Inoke Bainimarama highlighted this during their Annual 5KM Pink Walk at Albert Park this morning, saying the event is not just a walk but an important platform for raising awareness.
item.content:encoded:
Since January this year, 217 people have turned to the Fiji Cancer Society after being diagnosed with cancer, a number that continues to rise year after year.

Fiji Cancer Society Board member Inoke Bainimarama highlighted this during their Annual 5KM Pink Walk at Albert Park this morning, saying the event is not just a walk but an important platform for raising awareness.

Bainimarama says this year’s theme is “Turning Awareness into Action”, and he acknowledged everyone who turned up to support the cause.

More than 270 people, young and old, braved the rainy Suva weather this morning to take part in the walk, while another 220 people participated simultaneously in Lautoka.

He says they were delighted to have sponsors and more than 15 organisations represented at the event, as well as students, including members of the Suva Grammar School First XV.

Bainimarama also acknowledged cancer survivors who participated in the walk, saying they are at the forefront of the Society’s advocacy work.

He says they want to use the month of October to draw greater attention to cancer and raise awareness, particularly about breast cancer.

item.title: Local joint replacement surgery could be introduced as younger Fijians face joint damage - Dr McCaig
item.description: Joint replacement surgery is no longer reserved for the elderly, with younger Fijians increasingly requiring new hips and knees because of obesity, sports injuries, road crashes and previous joint damage. Pacific Specialist Healthcare (PSH) orthopaedic specialist and consultant Dr Vaigalo Eddie McCaig says joint problems can affect people across all age groups, with some younger patients already e
item.content:encoded:
Joint replacement surgery is no longer reserved for the elderly, with younger Fijians increasingly requiring new hips and knees because of obesity, sports injuries, road crashes and previous joint damage.

Pacific Specialist Healthcare (PSH) orthopaedic specialist and consultant Dr Vaigalo Eddie McCaig says joint problems can affect people across all age groups, with some younger patients already experiencing severe joint damage that may eventually require replacement surgery.

He explains that osteoarthritis is the loss of cartilage which protects the joint.

The cartilage allows the bones to move smoothly, but once it wears away, the bones begin rubbing against each other, causing pain, stiffness and reduced mobility.

Dr McCaig says carrying excess weight over many years places additional stress on weight-bearing joints such as the hips and knees.

The issue is particularly relevant to Fiji and the wider Pacific, where changing lifestyles and increasing body weight are contributing to orthopaedic problems.

Age, however, is far from the only factor.

Dr McCaig says he recently treated a woman in her early 50s who suffered injuries in a 2018 car crash .

He says she had previously undergone a partial hip replacement but is now experiencing problems and may require a total hip replacement.

In another case, Dr McCaig says a 28-year-old rugby player dislocated his hip and underwent surgery in New Zealand .

The hip subsequently dislocated again and remained out of position for about a year, eventually resulting in severe arthritis .

He says it is not just the elderly person with osteoarthritis, it can affect anyone .

With joint problems affecting patients across different age groups, PSH is looking at introducing joint replacement surgery at its hospitals in the future.

Dr McCaig says this could give patients access to treatment and follow-up care locally, reducing the need to travel overseas for surgery.

He stresses, however, that an X-ray alone should never determine whether a patient requires joint replacement.

He says surgery should always be the last option.

Dr McCaig says the operation itself is only one part of successful treatment, with proper follow-up and the management of potential complications also critical.

He also identified sports trauma, road crashes, infections, diabetes and HIV as major considerations in orthopaedic care.

For patients with diabetes or HIV, Dr McCaig says the risk of complications, including problems with wound healing, can increase significantly.

He says while an X-ray can show the extent of joint damage, it is the pain, reduced mobility and impact on a person's quality of life that should ultimately guide decisions about joint replacement.

item.title: Chand family gets fresh start after losing home in fire 2 yrs ago
item.description: The new home, built at a cost of more than $48,000 under Scheme 2 of the Government's Rural Housing Assistance Programme, was commissioned by Minister for Rural and Maritime Development and Disaster Management Mosese Bulitavu. Chand says his family lost everything in the fire and had been living with relatives for the past two years.
item.content:encoded:
The new home, built at a cost of more than $48,000 under Scheme 2 of the Government's Rural Housing Assistance Programme, was commissioned by Minister for Rural and Maritime Development and Disaster Management Mosese Bulitavu.

Chand says his family lost everything in the fire and had been living with relatives for the past two years.

He says it has not been easy, and the new house means his family can finally have a place of their own and begin rebuilding their lives.

Chand says the assistance came at an important time and has given his family a second chance to become homeowners.

He also thanked the people of Belego for supporting his family by helping them raise their one-third contribution towards the housing project.

Chand is encouraging families in rural and maritime communities who may need similar assistance to visit the nearest Ministry district office and enquire about the programmes available to them.

Bulitavu says the completion of the house is an example of how Government assistance can make a direct difference in the lives of families.

He says the Rural Housing Assistance Programme is particularly important for rural families who may face difficulties building or rebuilding their homes.

Bulitavu adds a home provides safety, security and dignity, and programmes such as the Rural Housing Assistance Programme can help families get back on their feet after difficult circumstances.

item.title: Vision Group records $375M annual revenue as Patel calls for faster government approvals
item.description: It was also highlighted that for the financial year that ended in March, the group reported a net profit after tax of $17.67 million, total assets of $314 million and equity of $141.8 million. Kamikamica has also revealed that there have been discussions between the stock exchanges of Fiji and Papua New Guinea to create a dual listing.
item.content:encoded:
It was also highlighted that for the financial year that ended in March, the group reported a net profit after tax of $17.67 million, total assets of $314 million and equity of $141.8 million.

Kamikamica has also revealed that there have been discussions between the stock exchanges of Fiji and Papua New Guinea to create a dual listing.

He says the software between the two exchanges is compatible and the proposal is now largely a matter for regulators.

Kamikamica says if the dual listing happens in the next few years, it could bring a different dimension to the South Pacific Stock Exchange by allowing capital to move between two of the largest economies in the Pacific.

He says it could also pave the way for other Pacific countries to become involved in the South Pacific Stock Exchange.

He also responded to Patel's comments on the ease of doing business, saying the Government has launched the first National Ease of Doing Business Strategy, with a target for 70 to 80 percent of government services to be automated by 2030.

He says this will include a National ID and the automation of immigration services.

Kamikamica says the Government is also working on a Building Permit Approval System, which was initially expected to be launched this year but may now be delayed until early next year.

He says the system is expected to reduce building permit approval times, which can currently take two to three years, to six months and eventually even shorter.

Kamikamica has encouraged Vision Group to continue focusing on innovation, sustainability and responsible investment as it enters the next decade as a listed company.

item.title: Fiji prepares for evolving terrorism and security threats with launch of Counter Terrorism Strategy 2026–2030
item.description: Fiji is stepping up preparations to address terrorism and emerging security threats, despite the Government saying a terrorist attack remains unlikely in the foreseeable future. This is at the centre of Fiji’s new Counter Terrorism Strategy 2026–2030, launched at the Grand Pacific Hotel in Suva.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji is stepping up preparations to address terrorism and emerging security threats, despite the Government saying a terrorist attack remains unlikely in the foreseeable future.

This is at the centre of Fiji’s new Counter Terrorism Strategy 2026–2030, launched at the Grand Pacific Hotel in Suva.

Minister for Policing and Communications Ioane Naivalurua says Fiji must prepare while the country remains at peace, stressing that unlikely does not mean impossible.

Naivalurua says the nature of terrorism and violent extremism has changed, with radicalisation able to occur online, extremist ideas spreading rapidly and violence potentially emerging from individual grievances with little warning.

He says the strategy is about protecting Fiji’s people, communities and institutions, while preserving the peace for future generations.

Naivalurua says Fiji will not tolerate terrorism or violent extremism from any direction, regardless of ideology, motivation or justification.

However, he says counterterrorism measures must remain principled and cannot become a basis for discrimination or suspicion based on religion, ethnicity, village, language or belief.

Naivalurua say Fiji’s response will remain grounded in the Constitution, rule of law, human rights, due process, necessity, proportionality and accountability.

He says counterterrorism is not simply a policing responsibility but a national responsibility, requiring cooperation between government agencies, security institutions, communities, schools, traditional and faith leaders, financial institutions, the technology sector and international partners.

The strategy is built around four pillars - prevention, preparation, response and recovery.

Naivalurua says prevention will focus on identifying and reducing risks before they become threats, while preparation will ensure government, security agencies and critical sectors are ready before a crisis occurs.

He says response will focus on protecting life, containing threats and restoring public safety, while recovery will involve restoring confidence, supporting affected communities and learning from incidents.

Naivalurua says the Government is also developing a Counterterrorism and Suppression of Terrorism Financing Bill with relevant agencies and international partners.

He says the legislation will strengthen Fiji’s legal capacity while ensuring counterterrorism action remains consistent with the Constitution, rule of law and human rights.

Naivalurua says Fiji’s security is also closely linked to the wider Pacific, with the country continuing to work with regional neighbours and international partners on intelligence sharing, border security, financial intelligence, cyber resilience and operational cooperation.

Meanwhile, US Embassy Chargé d’Affaires Christina Cavallo says threats today cross borders and increasingly move online, making preparedness a shared responsibility.

Cavallo says no single agency can address these threats alone, with security requiring cooperation across government, law enforcement, faith and community leaders, the private sector and international partners.

She says the new strategy is more than a policy document, describing it as a statement of national resolve and a contribution to regional security.

Cavallo says the United States recognises Fiji’s leadership and is proud to stand alongside Fiji as it strengthens its counterterrorism framework.

She says the United States has provided significant support to Fiji in areas linked to security and resilience.

This includes US$500,000 in foreign military financing to strengthen communications capabilities for the Republic of Fiji Navy, which Cavallo says will help Fiji track and disrupt transnational crime and illegal fishing in its waters.

The United States has also committed US$5.14 million over five years to strengthen Fiji’s ability to detect and contain infectious disease outbreaks.

Through the Millennium Challenge Corporation, the U.S. has also advanced a US$12 million grant to design and study a compact programme aimed at supporting Fiji’s long-term economic development.

Cavallo says U.S. State Department law enforcement assistance programmes, both through the U.S. Embassy in Fiji and Washington, also helped make the launch of the Counter Terrorism Strategy possible.

She says the United States remains committed to Fiji’s security and prosperity and to strengthening cooperation with its Pacific partners.

The strategy will run until 2030 and will be reviewed annually.
